extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, judges, software developers, and readers interested in US patent-eligibility law
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether computer-implemented or business-method patent claims are patent-eligible under the Alice v. CLS Bank decision, applying the Mayo two-step framework and related Federal Circuit tests. The page explains standards for identifying abstract ideas, inventive concept, preemption concerns, and drafting pitfalls that lead to §101 invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-step framework (Alice formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Mayo framework (as adopted in Alice) to decide §101 issues: first determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas); if so, proceed to step two and determine whether the claim adds an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to 'significantly more' than the ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the page: 'In the first Mayo step, the court must determine whether the patent claim under examination contains an abstract idea... In the second step... determine whether the patent adds to the idea "something extra" that embodies an "inventive concept."' If no inventive concept exists (i.e., the addition is conventional, routine, or generic), the claim is invalid under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must include an 'inventive concept' — an element or combination of elements 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court explains that an inventive concept must be more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity and must contain 'additional substantive limitations that narrow, confine, or otherwise tie down the claim so that, in practical terms, it does not cover the full abstract idea itself.' Ordinary and customary use of a general-purpose computer is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Step requires determining whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea such as an algorithm, method of computation, or other general principle (e.g., intermediated settlement, risk hedging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion treats concepts like 'intermediated settlement' as abstract ideas. If the claim is directed to such an idea, proceed to inventive-concept analysis. The Court stated: 'First, we determine whether the claims at issue are directed to one of those patent-ineligible concepts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim would effectively preempt all uses of the fundamental concept (i.e., monopolize the abstract idea), since preemption of an abstract idea weighs strongly toward ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts consider whether a claim 'poses a risk of preempting an abstract idea.' The Federal Circuit plurality and Alice emphasize that claims that preempt future innovation by covering the abstract idea itself are not patentable. Field-of-use limitations that still effectively preempt are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer/recitation-of-computer anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely requiring or reciting a generic computer implementation (or adding words like 'apply it' or limiting to a particular technological environment) does not transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations from the opinion: 'A mere instruction to implement an abstract idea on a computer "cannot impart patent eligibility."' and 'the mere recitation of a generic computer cannot transform a patent-ineligible abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.' Limiting to a particular technological environment is also not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Circuit plurality four-step/preemption-focused test
rubrics_metrics.description: Plurality (Lourie) articulated a test: (1) determine whether the claimed invention fits within one of the four statutory classes (process, machine, manufacture, composition); (2) determine whether the claim poses a risk of preempting an abstract idea; (3) identify the fundamental concept at risk of preemption; (4) perform an 'inventive concept' analysis to see whether there is a genuine human contribution that adds substantive limitations narrowing the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plurality framed the 'balance of the claim' concept: the human contribution must 'contain[] additional substantive limitations that narrow, confine, or otherwise tie down the claim so that, in practical terms, it does not cover the full abstract idea itself.' The court also asked whether steps combined with an abstract idea are 'insignificant, conventional, or routine.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Circuit's specific limiting-criteria (four questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider these specific questions when testing whether claim elements meaningfully limit an abstract idea: (a) is the limitation necessary to every practical use of the abstract idea and therefore not truly limiting; (b) does it 'amount to more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by researchers in the field'; (c) is it a 'token or trivial limitation' (insignificant post-solution activity); (d) is it merely a field-of-use limitation where the claim still effectively preempts all uses within the stated field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These questions (from the Federal Circuit plurality) are practical heuristics for assessing whether purported limitations add anything substantive beyond the abstract idea itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory-class fit inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial technical/formal check: determine whether the claimed invention fits within one of the four classes in the statute: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the plurality's first analytical step. Fitting into a statutory class does not decide eligibility; it is the starting point before analyzing abstractness and inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: functional-objective claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely 'describe a problem, announce purely functional steps that purport to solve the problem, and recite standard computer operations' are deficient because they lack an inventive concept and preempt subsequent specific solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit Judge Bryson's description: such patents 'represent little more than functional descriptions of objectives, rather than inventive solutions.' Courts treat those as claiming abstract ideas and thus ineligible under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test (as advocated by some amici)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative test urged by some amici: software should be patentable only if it satisfies the machine-or-transformation (MOT) test—i.e., is tied to a particular machine or transforms an article into a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Free Software Foundation and others argued for the MOT test to block broad software patents, but the Supreme Court's Alice opinion adopts Mayo's framework rather than endorsing MOT as the exclusive test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of claim types under §101 (method/system/media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether method, system (computer/system), and computer-readable-media claims should be treated equivalently for §101 analysis—i.e., whether a system or medium claim that merely recites an abstract idea implemented on a computer is subject to the same eligibility limits as method claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit en banc asked whether these claim categories should be considered equivalent under §101; Alice treated system and media claims that merely required generic computer implementation as ineligible in similar fashion to method claims.
